title: The Spanish Tragedy
description: Kyd's revenge tragedy, the most popular play of its generation: the ghost of Don Andrea and the personified Revenge watch from above as Hieronimo, Knight Marshal of Spain, discovers that his son Horatio has been murdered by the prince Balthazar and Lorenzo, and — after his wife Isabella's suicide — avenges him by staging a play in which the murderers die, biting out his own tongue before stabbing himself.
plot_or_argument: Andrea's ghost, slain in battle by Balthazar, returns with Revenge to see justice done; Horatio is hanged in the arbour by Balthazar and Lorenzo; Hieronimo's madness, his laments, and the discovery of the murderers fill the middle acts; the play-within-the-play 'Soliman and Perseda' becomes the engine of revenge, and the survivors' blood ends the tragedy.
narrative_structure: A revenge tragedy framed by the choric ghost-and-Revenge, built on the discovery-and-delay pattern, and climaxing in the play within the play.
principal_characters: Hieronimo; Bel-Imperia; Horatio; Lorenzo; Balthazar; Isabella; the Ghost of Andrea; Revenge; Pedringano; Serberine; the Viceroy of Portugal
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of strong rhetorical set pieces — Hieronimo's laments and the additions of 1602 (probably by Jonson) — with the famous 'in a word' tableaux.
historical_context: Performed from about 1587 and printed in 1592; revived with additions in 1602; it established the revenge formula that Hamlet, Titus Andronicus, and the Jacobean revenge school all answer.
literary_significance: The fountainhead of Elizabethan revenge tragedy — the play that taught the English stage the ghost, the delay, and the play-within-the-play.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1592 (with additions of 1602 in later editions). Standard edition: The Spanish Tragedy, ed. Philip Edwards (Revels, 1959).

title: Campaspe
description: Lyly's court comedy of the painter's triumph: Alexander the Great, in love with his captive Campaspe, commissions her portrait from the painter Apelles — who falls in love with her himself; the emperor, discovering the mutual love, renounces her and gives the couple his blessing, proving himself 'Alexander' in magnanimity as in conquest.
plot_or_argument: Alexander's philosophers (Diogenes in his tub, Plato, Aristotle) and generals debate around the love affair; Apelles paints and conceals his love; the courtiers' plots to part the lovers fail; and the play ends with Alexander's renunciation and the painter's marriage, the emperor's 'discipline' the play's moral.
narrative_structure: A five-act classical comedy on the Italian model, built of debate scenes — the philosophers' wit, the generals' counsel — with the painter's studio as its centre.
principal_characters: Alexander; Campaspe; Apelles; Diogenes; Plato; Aristotle; Hephestion; Parmenio; Manes; Psyllus; the pages
meter_and_prosody: Prose throughout — the Euphuistic manner transferred to the stage — with the songs of the finale.
historical_context: Performed before Elizabeth I by the Children of Paul's and the Chapel children on the same day (1 January 1584) in the 'battle of the theatres' between the two boy companies; printed the same year.
literary_significance: The first English high comedy of the court — the play that founded the elegant, debating tradition Jonson and the Restoration inherited.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1584. Standard edition: The Complete Works of John Lyly, ed. R. Warwick Bond (Oxford, 1902).

title: Sapho and Phao
description: Lyly's mythological court comedy: the ferryman Phao, made beautiful by Venus, is loved by the queen Sapho; Venus, jealous of the queen she meant to humble, afflicts Phao with love of herself; and the play resolves through Cupid's arrows and Sybilla's lore into Sapho's triumph over Venus and the renunciation of Phao's love.
plot_or_argument: Venus, angered by Sapho's chastity, arms Cupid against her; the arrows misfire, Phao is loved and Sapho infatuated; the court's debates (between the scholars and the women) anatomize love; Sybilla's counsel and Venus's flight end the play with Sapho restored to rule and Phao banished from desire.
narrative_structure: A five-act mythological debate-comedy of the Ovidian type, with the low comedy of the pages and servants as counterpoint.
principal_characters: Sapho; Phao; Venus; Cupid; Sybilla; the court ladies; the scholars; the pages
meter_and_prosody: Prose of Euphuistic balance, with songs and the debate set pieces.
historical_context: Performed at court in 1584 and printed the same year; its Sapho is read as a mirror of Elizabeth I, and its love-psychology answers the Alençon courtship debates of the early 1580s.
literary_significance: The classic of the Elizabethan mythological court play — a genre in which the Queen's own image was negotiated on stage.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1584. Standard edition: The Complete Works of John Lyly, ed. R. Warwick Bond (Oxford, 1902).

title: Gallathea
description: Lyly's pastoral comedy of disguise and desire: to appease Neptune's demand for the fairest virgin of the land, the fathers of Gallathea and Phillida disguise both girls as boys; the two 'youths' fall in love with each other, and the play ends with Venus's promise that 'one of them' shall be transformed into a man — a resolution whose gender the text leaves teasingly open.
plot_or_argument: Neptune's sacrifice is evaded by the two disguises; the shepherds' loves and the fair's episodes (Rafe, Robin, and the alchemist) fill the middle; the 'boys'' mutual love complicates everything; and the final scene, with Diana and Venus contending, produces the metamorphosis promise and the virgin's reprieve.
narrative_structure: A five-act pastoral built on the cross-dressing device, with the fair scenes and Neptune's wrath as frame and counterpoint.
principal_characters: Gallathea; Phillida; Neptune; Venus; Diana; Cupid; the fathers (Tityrus and Melibeus); Hebe; the fair folk (Rafe, Robin, the Alchemist, the Mariner)
meter_and_prosody: Prose with verse for the divine scenes — the gods speak verse, the mortals prose, in Lyly's careful decorum.
historical_context: Probably performed at court on 1 January 1588, the Armada year; printed 1592; its same-sex desire, licensed by the boy actors' convention, has made it a touchstone of queer reading of the Renaissance stage.
literary_significance: The most daring of Lyly's gender comedies — the play in which the Elizabethan stage's play with sexual identity becomes the plot itself.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1592. Standard edition: The Complete Works of John Lyly, ed. R. Warwick Bond (Oxford, 1902).

title: Endymion
alternative_titles: Endymion, the Man in the Moon
description: Lyly's allegorical court comedy: Endymion's hopeless love for the moon-goddess Cynthia casts him into a forty-year sleep from which only her kiss can wake him; the intrigues of the sorceress Dipsas and the braggart Sir Tophas complicate the court, and the play ends with Endymion's awakening and the famous reading of Cynthia as the Queen whose 'virtue' the play mirrors.
plot_or_argument: Endymion renounces Tellus for Cynthia; Tellus's jealousy and Dipsas's enchantment cast him asleep; his friend Eumenides quests for the cure, and the riddle of the fountain directs him to the kiss; the sub-plot of Sir Tophas's mock-chivalry and the pages' comedy runs alongside; Cynthia's kiss wakes the sleeper, and the play closes on the praises of her constancy.
narrative_structure: A five-act court allegory with a fairy-tale centre (the sleep, the quest, the cure) and a burlesque chivalric sub-plot.
principal_characters: Endymion; Cynthia; Tellus; Eumenides; Semele; Dipsas; Sir Tophas; Geron; Corsites; the Fairies; the pages (Epiton, Samias, Dares)
meter_and_prosody: Prose for the court scenes, verse for the enchantments and the finale, with the songs of the fairies.
historical_context: Performed at court in 1588 and printed in 1591; the play's veiled allusions to Leicester's fall and the Queen's favour have kept its allegory a critical puzzle for four centuries.
literary_significance: The most influential of the Elizabethan court allegories — the model of the dream-play of royal favour and disfavour.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1591. Standard edition: The Complete Works of John Lyly, ed. R. Warwick Bond (Oxford, 1902).

title: Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay
description: Greene's romantic comedy of Oxford magic and Suffolk love: Friar Bacon, England's great magician, works his brazen head and his glass of distant seeing while the Prince of Wales, the earls, and the keeper's daughter Margaret of Fressingfield play out their love-plot — the play moving between the scholars' cell and the country fair to its double ending of broken magic and honest marriage.
plot_or_argument: Prince Edward and Lacy both love Margaret; Lacy woos her in the prince's name and wins her for himself; the prince's rage, the rivals' duel, and the disguises of the middle acts complicate the match; Bacon's glass shows the fathers' deaths and is shattered; the brazen head speaks 'Time is, Time was, Time is past' and falls; and the play ends with the marriages and the friar's renunciation of magic.
narrative_structure: A two-world comedy — the university cell and the Fressingfield household — braided by the magic glass, in Greene's most accomplished construction.
principal_characters: Friar Bacon; Friar Bungay; Prince Edward; Lacy, Earl of Lincoln; Margaret of Fressingfield; the Keeper; Miles; the two scholars (the sons of Lambert and Serlsby); the Devil (in the conjuring); the brazen head
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse for the court and scholars, prose for the rustics — the mixed style that became the Elizabethan comic norm.
historical_context: Performed about 1589 and printed in 1594; its Oxford setting and national hero-magician answered the vogue for conjuring plays after Faustus.
literary_significance: The masterpiece of the University Wits' romantic comedy — the play in which magic, love, and England's own legends met on the popular stage.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1594. Standard edition: Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay, ed. J. A. Lavin (New Mermaids, 1969).

title: James IV
alternative_titles: The Scottish History of James the Fourth
description: Greene's Scottish romance-play: King James IV of Scotland, married to Dorothea, falls in love with the English lady Ida and plots his queen's murder; Dorothea escapes in disguise, is saved by the English knight Sir Eustace and nursed back to health, and the play ends with the king's repentance, the recognition scene, and the reunion — a history play turned romance, framed by the chorus of Oberon and the fairies.
plot_or_argument: James, corrupted by the flatterer Ateukin, orders Dorothea's death; the honest lords refuse and the queen flees in disguise; wounded, she is healed by Lady Anderson; the wars with England and the king's remorse lead to the final scene, where the disguised queen reveals herself and all is forgiven in the play's comedy of errors and recognitions.
narrative_structure: A five-act romance on a chronicle frame, with the fairy induction and interludes of Oberon, and the Anderson sub-plot as the comic engine of the recognition.
principal_characters: King James IV of Scotland; Queen Dorothea; Ida; Sir Eustace; Ateukin; Lady Anderson; Sir Cuthbert Anderson; the Bishop of St Andrews; Oberon; the fairies
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse with prose for the comic scenes, and the fairies' songs in the induction.
historical_context: Printed in 1598 and performed about 1590; its Scottish matter predates James VI's accession to the English throne, and its 'history' is romance from the first.
literary_significance: The bridge between the chronicle play and Shakespearean romance — the play in which Greene's pastoral art and the history vogue met.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1598. Standard edition: The Scottish History of James the Fourth, ed. Norman Sanders (Revels, 1970).

title: The Arraignment of Paris
description: Peele's pastoral-mythological court play: the shepherd Paris, commanded by the gods, judges the beauty contest of Juno, Pallas, and Venus; he awards the golden apple to Venus, whose bribe is the love of the nymph Oenone, and the play ends — after the goddesses' appeal — with Diana's famous judgment awarding the apple to 'Eliza', the Queen herself, a 'nymph' above all the goddesses.
plot_or_argument: At the wedding feast of Peleus and Thetis, Discord casts the golden apple; Paris, in his pastoral solitude with Oenone, receives the task of judgment; the three goddesses plead their cases in set speeches; Paris judges Venus; the goddesses appeal to the Olympian court; and Diana's final verdict transfers the prize to Eliza, flattering the Queen beyond the myth.
narrative_structure: A masque-like pastoral in five acts, built on the judgment set piece and the appeals, with the shepherd scenes of Colin and the nymphs as pastoral interludes.
principal_characters: Paris; Oenone; Juno; Pallas; Venus; Diana; Eliza (Elizabeth I); Colin; Hobbinol; Thenot; the shepherds and nymphs
meter_and_prosody: Mixed verse forms — blank verse, rhyme, and songs — with the pageantry of the goddesses' entries.
historical_context: Performed by the Children of the Chapel before the Queen about 1581–84 and printed in 1584; its compliment to Elizabeth made Peele's name at court.
literary_significance: The founding text of the Elizabethan court pastoral and of the genre of the Queen's mythological flattery.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1584. Standard edition: The Life and Works of George Peele, gen. ed. Charles Tyler Prouty, 3 vols (Yale, 1952–70).

title: The Old Wives' Tale
description: Peele's folkloric comedy of enchantment: three pages lost in the woods take shelter with the smith Clunch, and the old wife Madge's fireside tale comes alive around them — the brothers seeking their sister Delia, the sorcerer Sacrapant's enchantments, the grateful dead man Jack, and the 'white bear of England's wood' — until the tale's happy ending dissolves back into the night.
plot_or_argument: Madge's rambling tale is staged as she tells it: the wandering knights, the enchanted well that turns heads, the harvesters' song, Huanebango and Corebus's comic quests, and the rescue of Delia from Sacrapant's spells, with the dead man's gratitude and the bear's aid — the whole framed by the pages' bewildered watching.
narrative_structure: A frame-and-tale structure unique in Elizabethan drama: the story is performed as the old wife invents it, with the boundaries between teller, tale, and audience deliberately porous.
principal_characters: Madge (the old wife); Clunch; the three pages; Sacrapant; Delia; the two brothers; Jack (the grateful dead man); Huanebango; Corebus; the white bear; the harvesters
meter_and_prosody: Mixed verse and prose, with the harvesters' song — 'Whenas the rye reach to the chin' — as its remembered lyric.
historical_context: Written about 1591–93 and printed in 1595; it parodies the romances and enchantments of the popular stage (including Greene's and Peele's own) in the manner of a native Arabian Nights.
literary_significance: The most delightful of the English enchantment plays — a folk-tale theatre that Milton remembered when he wrote Comus.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1595. Standard edition: The Old Wives' Tale, ed. Patricia Binnie (Revels, 1980).

title: Summer's Last Will and Testament
description: Nashe's one surviving solo play, a summer show performed at Archbishop Whitgift's palace at Croydon: Summer, dying of the plague-year's sickness, makes his will and bequeaths the world to Autumn and Winter, while the seasons, the personified vices, and the jester Will Summer pass in review — the play's songs ('Adieu, farewell, earth's bliss') and its memento mori making it the great plague elegy of the Elizabethan stage.
plot_or_argument: Summer, sick and dying, summons his officers — Ver (Spring), Solstitium, and the rest — to account for the year; the debate of the seasons, the entertainment of the Harvest lord, and the pageant of the vices fill the show; Summer makes his will, bequeathing the world to the colder seasons, and dies, with the songs and the jester's epilogue closing the play on mortality itself.
narrative_structure: A masque-like entertainment of pageants, debates, and songs, loose in structure but unified by the dying Summer's progress to his will and death.
principal_characters: Summer; Autumn; Winter; Ver (Spring); Solstitium; Bacchus; Harvest; Will Summer (the jester); the satyrs; the nymphs; Death (in the songs)
meter_and_prosody: Mixed verse and prose, with the famous lyric 'Adieu, farewell, earth's bliss' ('A Litany in Time of Plague') as its summit.
historical_context: Performed at Croydon in the plague summer of 1592 (perhaps September), for the Archbishop of Canterbury's household; printed in 1600.
literary_significance: The great plague poem of the English Renaissance and Nashe's masterpiece of the mixed mode — masque, satire, and elegy in one.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1600. Standard edition: The Works of Thomas Nashe, ed. R. B. McKerrow, 5 vols (1904–10; rev. F. P. Wilson, 1958).

title: Bussy D'Ambois
description: Chapman's tragedy of heroic virtue at court: the poor gentleman Bussy d'Ambois, raised by the Duke of Anjou to the French court, defies the great, wins the love of the married Tamyra, and is destroyed by her husband Montsurry's trap — dying on his feet, propped against the wall, 'like a Roman' whose spirit cannot be killed.
plot_or_argument: Bussy arrives at court in poverty and virtue, quarrels and triumphs with the courtiers, and is loved by Tamyra; the friar's conjuring reveals the affair to Montsurry; the revenge plot — the summoned spirits, the forced confession, the ambush — kills the friar and corners Bussy; his death speech turns defeat into apotheosis, and Tamyra's final letters close the tragedy.
narrative_structure: A five-act Senecan tragedy of the heroic mode, with the friar's necromancy and the spirits (Behemoth and the rest) as its supernatural machinery.
principal_characters: Bussy d'Ambois; Tamyra; Montsurry; the Duke of Anjou (Monsieur); the King of France; the Guise; the Friar; Pero; Behemoth and the spirits
meter_and_prosody: Chapman's dense, oracular blank verse — packed with stoic sententiae — reaching its height in Bussy's death speech.
historical_context: Based on the historical Bussy (d. 1579) as reported in French chronicles; performed about 1604 and printed in 1607, with a revised text in 1641.
literary_significance: The great English tragedy of heroic self-assertion — the play in which the Renaissance individual asserts himself against the court and the stars.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1607. Standard edition: Bussy D'Ambois, ed. Nicholas Brooke (Revels, 1964).

title: Eastward Ho
description: The city comedy of 1605 by Chapman, Jonson, and Marston: the goldsmith's virtuous apprentice Golding prospers while the prodigal Quicksilver and the usurer Security speculate their way toward Virginia; Quicksilver's voyage ends in shipwreck on the Isle of Dogs and the counter, and the play ends with the prodigal's repentance — though not before its satire of the Scots landed the authors in prison.
plot_or_argument: Touchstone the goldsmith divides his world between the good apprentice and the bad; Quicksilver drinks, cheats, and embarks for Virginia; the storms, the shipwreck, and the counter follow; Golding marries Touchstone's daughter and prospers; and the final scene distributes justice, mercy, and the play's famous verdicts on London's vices.
narrative_structure: A five-act city comedy on the Jonsonian model, with the Virginia voyage as its satirical engine and the last act's trial-and-pardon as its resolution.
principal_characters: Touchstone; Golding; Quicksilver; Security; Mistress Touchstone; Gertrude; Mildred; Sir Petronel Flash; Winifred; Sindefy; the Captain; the Scrivener
meter_and_prosody: Prose and blank verse in the collaborative mix, with Quicksilver's repentant ballad in the counter as its remembered set piece.
historical_context: Performed by the Children of the Queen's Revels in 1605; its gibes at the new Scots courtiers offended James I, and Chapman and Jonson were imprisoned for it — Marston escaping arrest — the most famous censorship case of the Jacobean stage.
literary_significance: The great satire of Jacobean London's money-madness and colonial fever — a collaboration of the age's three sharpest pens.
attribution_notes: Jointly by Chapman, Jonson, and Marston, as stated in the stationers' records; the division of scenes is partly conjectural.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1605. Standard edition: Eastward Ho, ed. C. G. Petter (New Mermaids, 1973).

title: The White Devil
description: Webster's first independent tragedy, of the Italian court: Vittoria Corombona, married to Camillo, loves Duke Brachiano, whose wife Isabella is murdered by the lovers' plot; Vittoria's great trial for her husband's death follows, then the revenge of Isabella's brother Francisco — poisoned portrait, masque of murderers, and the final bloodbath in which Brachiano, Vittoria, and her brother Flamineo all die.
plot_or_argument: Flamineo panders his sister to Brachiano; Isabella and Camillo are murdered; Vittoria's arraignment — 'I am summoned to appear before the wolf' — is the play's trial centrepiece; the counterfeit letter and Francisco's disguised revenges pursue the lovers; and the last act's masque of revengers kills Brachiano, with Vittoria and Flamineo dying in the mutual treachery of the close.
narrative_structure: A five-act revenge tragedy of the Italian court, built on the trial scene and the double masque, with the choric comments of the ambassadors and the ghost of Isabella.
principal_characters: Vittoria Corombona; Flamineo; Duke Brachiano; Francisco de Medici; Cardinal Monticelso; Isabella; Camillo; Cornelia; Marcello; Zanche; Lodovico; Gasparo; the Ambassadors
meter_and_prosody: Webster's dark, emblematic blank verse — the arraignment speeches and the dirges are its heights — with the prose of the panders as counterpoint.
historical_context: Based on the historical Vittoria Accoramboni (d. 1585); performed at the Red Bull in 1612 to a hostile audience, as Webster complains in his preface; printed the same year.
literary_significance: One of the two masterpieces (with The Duchess of Malfi) of Jacobean tragedy — the play that defined Webster's theatre of corruption and splendour.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1612. Standard edition: The White Devil, ed. John Russell Brown (Revels, 1960).

title: The Duchess of Malfi
description: Webster's tragedy of the widowed Duchess who remarries her steward Antonio against her brothers' will: the 'Aragonian brethren' — the twisted Ferdinand and the corrupt Cardinal — pursue her with spies, imprisonment, and madmen's masques until her murder by strangling; the play then turns to the revenges that destroy the brothers, ending with the famous line, 'Cover her face; mine eyes dazzle; she died young'.
plot_or_argument: The Duchess secretly marries Antonio and bears children; Bosola, the malcontent spy, discovers the truth; Ferdinand's fury and the Cardinal's policy drive the persecution — the wax corpses, the madmen, the executioners; the Duchess dies with her dignity ('I am Duchess of Malfi still'); and Bosola's belated revenges kill Ferdinand, the Cardinal, and himself in the final bloodbath.
narrative_structure: A five-act tragedy in two movements — the Duchess's love and martyrdom, then the revengers' self-destruction — with the echo scene and the madmen's masque as its set pieces.
principal_characters: the Duchess of Malfi; Antonio Bologna; Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria; the Cardinal; Bosola; Delio; Cariola; Julia; Pescara; the Doctor; the madmen
meter_and_prosody: The summit of Webster's blank verse — the wooing scene, the prison scene, and the dirges — with the malcontent prose of Bosola as its instrument of irony.
historical_context: Based on the story of Giovanna d'Aragona (d. 1510) via Painter's Palace of Pleasure; performed about 1614 by the King's Men at Blackfriars and the Globe; printed in 1623.
literary_significance: Generally ranked the greatest non-Shakespearean tragedy of the English stage — the supreme study of courage under persecution.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1623. Standard edition: The Duchess of Malfi, ed. John Russell Brown (Revels, 1964).

title: A Mad World, My Masters
description: Middleton's early city comedy of tricks: the rake Follywit, disguised as a lord and then as a player, gulls his rich grandfather Sir Bounteous Progress; the courtesan Frank Gullman is passed off as a virgin; and the bawdy plot of Penitent Brothel and the Harebrain household runs alongside — the whole a 'mad world' of disguises whose final scene dissolves into the play-within-the-play of The Slip.
plot_or_argument: Follywit robs his grandfather three times over in three disguises; the gullings of the 'virgin' Gullman and the jealousy comedy of Harebrain interweave; the final robbery turns into the play performed before Sir Bounteous, who is robbed as he watches — the trick revealed only in the last lines, when Follywit marries Gullman with his grandfather's blessing.
narrative_structure: A five-act intrigue of triple disguise built on the trick-play device, with the play-within-the-play as its climactic joke on the audience as well as the gull.
principal_characters: Follywit; Sir Bounteous Progress; Frank Gullman; Penitent Brothel; Harebrain; Mistress Harebrain; the Succubus (appearing as Mistress Harebrain); the players
meter_and_prosody: Prose and verse in Middleton's swift, sardonic mix, with the mock-tragedy of the players as its final parody.
historical_context: Performed by the Children of Paul's in 1605 and printed in 1608; its frank bawdry answered the fashion of the private-theatre comedies.
literary_significance: The wittiest of Middleton's early comedies — a laboratory of the trick-plot and the play-within-the-play he would perfect.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1608. Standard edition: Thomas Middleton: The Collected Works, gen. eds Gary Taylor and John Lavagnino (Oxford, 2007).

title: A Chaste Maid in Cheapside
description: Middleton's comedy of London's sexual economy: the goldsmith Yellowhammer's daughter Moll, betrothed by her parents to the decadent knight Sir Walter Whorehound, loves the poor Touchwood Junior; the city's trades in food, sex, and legitimacy — the Allwits' household, the promoters, the puritans feasting at a christening — fill the play, until Sir Walter's ruin and Moll's mock-death restore the lovers.
plot_or_argument: Sir Walter finances the Allwits and fathers their 'children' while courting Moll; Touchwood Senior's fertility and his brother's love-plot run through the middle acts; the christening feast and the arrest of the gallants expose the city's corruptions; and the final scene, with Moll's pretended death and revival, joins the lovers and topples the knight.
narrative_structure: A five-act cross-section of Cheapside — multiple households joined by Sir Walter's purse — in Middleton's most populous and corrosive comic design.
principal_characters: Moll Yellowhammer; Touchwood Junior; Touchwood Senior; Sir Walter Whorehound; Yellowhammer; Maudlin Yellowhammer; the Allwits; the Kixes; the promoters; the wench; the puritans
meter_and_prosody: Prose and verse of Middleton's quickest, cruellest wit, with the christening scene's hypocritical feasting as its summit.
historical_context: Performed by the Lady Elizabeth's Men at the Swan in 1613 and printed in 1630; its satire of the Jacobean marriage market and puritan hypocrisy is the most scathing of the age.
literary_significance: The sharpest of the Jacobean city comedies — a play that makes money, sex, and religion a single system of exchange.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1630. Standard edition: Thomas Middleton: The Collected Works, gen. eds Gary Taylor and John Lavagnino (Oxford, 2007).

title: Women Beware Women
description: Middleton's tragedy of Florence: Bianca, married in flight to the merchant's factor Leantio, is seduced by the Duke — Leantio watching from the balcony in the play's most infamous scene — while the parallel plot of Isabella and the incestuous Hippolito (her uncle) runs alongside; the play ends in the masque of revenges in which the Duke, Bianca, and the whole company die by poison, trap, and sword.
plot_or_argument: Bianca's elopement, the Duke's lust, and Livia's pandering destroy the Leantio household; Hippolito's incestuous love and Livia's matchmaking destroy the Ward's marriage-plot; the final masque — prepared as entertainment — becomes the engine of mutual revenge, killing the Duke, Bianca, Hippolito, Livia, and the rest in a cascade of 'justice' that spares no one.
narrative_structure: A double plot of seduction and revenge converging in the masque of Act 5, with Livia's chess game — the moves paralleling the seduction — as the play's most celebrated device.
principal_characters: Bianca; Leantio; the Duke of Florence; Livia; Hippolito; Isabella; the Ward; Guardiano; Fabritio; the Cardinal; the Mother
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of Middleton's most controlled bitterness, with the masque's spectacle and the chess scene as its formal coups.
historical_context: Based loosely on the Bianca Cappello story via Malespini; written about 1621 and printed only in 1657; its chess scene is the most famous stage metaphor of Jacobean seduction.
literary_significance: Middleton's tragic masterpiece — the darkest anatomy of marriage, lust, and commodified womanhood on the Jacobean stage.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1657. Standard edition: Thomas Middleton: The Collected Works, gen. eds Gary Taylor and John Lavagnino (Oxford, 2007).

title: The Changeling
description: Middleton and Rowley's tragedy of desire and madness: Beatrice-Joanna, betrothed to Alonzo but in love with Alsemero, commissions the ugly servant De Flores to murder her fiancé; his price is her virginity, and the play follows the pair's descent through murder, the bed-trick with the maid Diaphanta, and madness to the final deaths — while the comic sub-plot of the madhouse, where the pretended fools and madmen perform, doubles the theme of 'change'.
plot_or_argument: De Flores kills Alonzo and claims Beatrice-Joanna; the wedding to Alsemero proceeds through the virginity-test and the Diaphanta substitution; the castle catches fire (in the plot), the murders of Diaphanta and the witnesses follow, and the final scene's confessions — Beatrice-Joanna's 'I am that of your blood was taken from you' — end with the lovers' deaths and the madhouse's ironic close.
narrative_structure: A two-plot structure unique in the canon: the main tragic plot (by Middleton) and the madhouse comedy (by Rowley) run in deliberate counterpoint, never meeting until the thematic rhyme of the final scene.
principal_characters: Beatrice-Joanna; De Flores; Alsemero; Alonzo de Piracquo; Tomazo de Piracquo; Vermandero; Diaphanta; Jasperino; the madhouse crew (Alibius, Lollio, Antonio, Franciscus, Isabella)
meter_and_prosody: Middleton's verse in the main plot — swift, ironic, and chilling — against Rowley's prose farce in the madhouse.
historical_context: Performed by the Lady Elizabeth's Men in 1622, at court in 1624, and printed in 1653; based on Reynolds's God's Revenge Against Murder (1621).
literary_significance: One of the great Jacobean tragedies — the study of complicity and self-loss ('the deed's creature') that T. S. Eliot would single out as the age's masterpiece of moral horror.
attribution_notes: Middleton (main plot) and William Rowley (madhouse sub-plot) as stated on the title page; the division is uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1653. Standard edition: The Changeling, ed. N. W. Bawcutt (Revels, 1958).

title: The Shoemaker's Holiday
description: Dekker's comedy of London's craftsmen: the shoemaker Simon Eyre rises from journeyman to Lord Mayor of London, his shop becomes the scene of the play's feasts and jests, and the love-plot of the disguised nobleman Lacy ('Hans the shoemaker') and the Lord Mayor's daughter Rose runs to its happy ending — the play ending with Eyre's feast for all the 'prentices of London and the king's own visit to the shop.
plot_or_argument: Lacy, nephew of the Earl of Lincoln, refuses the arranged marriage and disguises himself as a Dutch shoemaker to serve Eyre and woo Rose; Eyre's fortunes rise through a lucky cargo to the mayoralty; the lovers are discovered and the earl's opposition overcome; and the Shrove Tuesday feast crowns the comedy with the king's blessing on the gentle craft.
narrative_structure: A five-act citizen comedy in the romantic mode, with the shop as its centre and the rise of Eyre as its civic plot.
principal_characters: Simon Eyre; Margery Eyre; Lacy (Hans); Rose Oatley; Sir Roger Oatley; the Earl of Lincoln; Firk; Hodge; Ralph Damport; Jane; Hammon; the King
meter_and_prosody: Prose and blank verse in Dekker's warmest register, with the shoemakers' songs and the feast scenes as its set pieces.
historical_context: Performed by the Admiral's Men in 1599 and printed in 1600; its craftsmen's holiday and its king's visit celebrated the civic culture of London on the eve of the century's turn.
literary_significance: The classic of the citizen comedy — the play that gave the London trades their theatre, and the ancestor of the sentimental comedy of the next centuries.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1600. Standard edition: The Shoemaker's Holiday, ed. R. L. Smallwood and Stanley Wells (Revels, 1979).

title: The Honest Whore, Part 1
description: Dekker and Middleton's comedy of conversion: the courtesan Bellafront, courted by all Milan, is converted to virtue by the grief of her rejected suitor Hippolito; the madhouse of Bethlehem, where her father Anselmo feigns madness to save her, supplies the play's great scene; and the play ends with her marriage to the patient Matheo — the first part of the diptych continued in Part 2 (c. 1605).
plot_or_argument: Bellafront plies her trade until Hippolito's lament and her father's disguise break her heart; her conversion, the testing of her suitors, and the schemes of the pander and the courtiers follow; the scene in Bedlam, with the madmen's pageant of the city's vices, is the play's moral centre; and the final act restores Bellafront to marriage and her father to peace.
narrative_structure: A five-act comedy of conversion built on the two great set pieces — the madhouse and the conversion — with the Duke's disguised progress through the city as frame.
principal_characters: Bellafront; Hippolito; Matheo; Anselmo (disguised as the madman); Candido the linen-draper; the Duke of Milan; Infelice; Fluello; Castruccio; Pioratto; the madmen of Bedlam
meter_and_prosody: Prose and verse in the two authors' distinct registers, with the madmen's speeches as the play's most quoted passages.
historical_context: Performed by Prince Henry's Men in 1604 and printed the same year; the Bedlam scene answered the vogue for madhouse shows, and the play's reform of the whore answered the city's moralists.
literary_significance: The great Elizabethan-Jacobean comedy of conversion — the play that made the 'honest whore' a type of the English stage's moral theatre.
attribution_notes: By Dekker and Middleton jointly, as printed; the division of scenes is debated.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1604. Standard edition: The Dramatic Works of Thomas Dekker, ed. Fredson Bowers, 4 vols (Cambridge, 1953–61).

title: The Atheist's Tragedy
description: Tourneur's tragedy of providence: the atheist D'Amville murders his brother to advance his house, plots the ruin of his nephew Charlemont and the rape of his niece Castabella, and is finally killed by his own axe — striking his own brains out as he raises it against his son's head — in a play whose argument is the certainty of divine justice, staged against the atheist's every calculation.
plot_or_argument: D'Amville kills Montferrers and blames bandits; Charlemont is sent to the wars and believed dead; the uncle's schemes against Castabella and his own sons proceed; the ghost of Montferrers appears, the counter-plots of the villains fail one by one; and the last act's trial and the accidental suicide of D'Amville ('the justice of God') complete the demonstration, with the lovers' marriage as the play's reward.
narrative_structure: A five-act tragedy of providence built as a counter-argument to the revenge play — the wronged hero refuses revenge, and heaven's engines work without him.
principal_characters: D'Amville; Charlemont; Castabella; Montferrers (the Ghost); Levidulcia; Sebastian; Rousard; Borachio; Snuffe; the Puritan chaplain Languebeau Snuffe
meter_and_prosody: A harsh, emblematic blank verse with the sententious choruses of the play's moral argument.
historical_context: Printed in 1611 with a dedication to Sir Walter Chute; it answered the decade's revenge vogue with an anti-revenge tragedy, and its atheist answered the Marlovian overreachers.
literary_significance: The great counter-revenge tragedy of the Jacobean stage — the play that turned the genre's own machinery against the atheism it usually indulged.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1611. Standard edition: The Atheist's Tragedy, ed. Irving Ribner (Revels, 1964).

title: The Revenger's Tragedy
description: The great anonymous (formerly Tourneur, now generally Middleton) revenge tragedy: Vindice, whose beloved was poisoned by the old Duke for resisting him, revenges her by the poisoned skull trick — the Duke kissing the painted, poisoned lips of the skull he thinks a country girl — and then by masquerading through the corrupt court to the final masque of revengers, in which the Duke's son and his faction die and Vindice himself, boasting, is condemned by his own confession.
plot_or_argument: Vindice and his brother Hippolito enter the Duke's service to destroy him; the skull of Gloriana, dressed and poisoned, kills the Duke in the 'bony lady' scene; the succession struggle of Lussurioso, Ambitioso, Supervacuo, and Spurio fills the middle acts; the final masque — revengers killing revengers — clears the stage; and Vindice's boast, 'we are ourselves our own revenge', delivers him and his brother to execution.
narrative_structure: A five-act revenge tragedy of accelerating symmetries, built on the skull device, the play-within-the-play of the masque, and the choric commentary of Vindice's soliloquies.
principal_characters: Vindice; Hippolito; the Duke; Lussurioso; Ambitioso; Supervacuo; Spurio; the Duchess; Gratiana; Castiza; Antonio; Piero; the skull of Gloriana
meter_and_prosody: A verse of savage brilliance — the openings ('Duke, royal lecher!') and the skull scene are its peaks — with the play's memento mori running through every act.
historical_context: Performed by the King's Men in 1606 and printed in 1607 without an author's name; attributed to Tourneur from 1656 until the twentieth century's stylistic case transferred it to Middleton.
literary_significance: The most extreme and most brilliant of the Jacobean revenge plays — a tragedy of skulls, lust, and self-consuming justice.
attribution_notes: Printed anonymously; long attributed to Cyril Tourneur, now generally assigned to Thomas Middleton on stylistic evidence; the question remains open in some scholarship.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1607/08. Standard edition: The Revenger's Tragedy, ed. Brian Gibbons (New Mermaids, 2nd edn, 1991); Thomas Middleton: The Collected Works (Oxford, 2007).

title: The Malcontent
description: Marston's tragicomedy of the displaced duke: Altofronto, deposed by his usurping brother Pietro, returns to court disguised as the malcontent Malevole, whose bitter truths scour the court of Genoa; through the intrigues of Mendoza, the play's machiavel, the plots double and reverse until the final scene's masque restores the true duke — and with him the play's satirical license.
plot_or_argument: Malevole haunts the usurper's court with truth-telling; Mendoza, the courtier, plots to seize the duchy, poisoning, banishing, and betraying in turn; the counter-plots of Malevole and the banished Pietro (in disguise) entangle the machiavel; and the final masque, with the deaths staged and revealed, restores Altofronto to his throne and pardons the penitent.
narrative_structure: A five-act tragicomedy built on the disguised-duke device, with the malcontent's satiric set pieces and the final masque of revelations.
principal_characters: Altofronto (Malevole); Pietro Jacomo; Mendoza; Aurelia; Ferneze; Celso; Bilioso; Maquerelle; Maria; the fools (Passarello)
meter_and_prosody: Marston's snarling, paradoxical verse for Malevole's truths, with prose for the court's baseness.
historical_context: Performed by the Children of the Chapel in 1604 and printed the same year; Webster supplied an induction for the King's Men's revival, and the play's 'malcontent' became the decade's signature type.
literary_significance: The play that named the Jacobean malcontent — the great satire of courtly corruption that Shakespeare answered in Measure for Measure.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1604 (with Webster's induction). Standard edition: The Malcontent, ed. G. K. Hunter (Revels, 1975).

title: The Dutch Courtesan
description: Marston's city comedy of appetite and virtue: the young gallant Freevill, about to marry the chaste Beatrice, casts off his mistress, the Dutch courtesan Franceschina, whose jealousy hires the pander Cocledemoy's 'murder' of him; the counterfeit death, the trial of the innocent Malheureux, and the final act's reversals end with the courtesan whipped and the lovers married — virtue triumphant over the city's flesh-markets.
plot_or_argument: Freevill's engagement and Franceschina's fury set the plot; Malheureux, the would-be virtuous friend, is tempted by the courtesan and trapped; the staged murder, the substitute corpse, and the trial scenes complicate the middle acts; and the final scene, with the 'dead' man's return, sentences Franceschina to the cart and the whip and marries the two honest couples.
narrative_structure: A five-act comedy of intrigue on the Jonsonian model, with the brothel scenes and the trial as the play's moral poles, and Cocledemoy's prose trickeries as its comic engine.
principal_characters: Freevill; Malheureux; Franceschina; Beatrice; Crispinella; Cocledemoy; Mulligrub; Mistress Mulligrub; Tysefew; Mary Faugh
meter_and_prosody: Prose for the London scenes and verse for the lovers, in Marston's sharpest comic register.
historical_context: Performed by the Children of the Queen's Revels in 1605 and printed the same year; its London scenes answered the city-comedy vogue of 1604–05.
literary_significance: Marston's best comedy — a satire of appetite whose frankness about sex and money tested the private theatre's licence.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1605. Standard edition: The Dutch Courtesan, ed. M. L. Wine (Regents, 1965).

title: Philaster
description: Beaumont and Fletcher's tragicomedy of the rightful heir: Philaster, prince of Sicily displaced by the usurper, loves the usurper's daughter Arethusa; his page Bellario (really the girl Euphrasia in disguise) is accused of adultery with her; and the play moves through the forest scenes, the attempted murders, and the double wounding to the final scene, where the king's lust is exposed, the lovers reconciled, and the kingdom restored to its prince.
plot_or_argument: Arethusa is betrothed to the boorish Pharamond but loves Philaster; the page Bellario's devotion and the court's slanders complicate the love; the hunting scene's wounds — Philaster stabbing Arethusa and himself — lead to the trial; the king's attempt on Bellario reveals Euphrasia's disguise; and the final act restores all, with the rebellious citizens of Sicily as the deus ex machina of justice.
narrative_structure: A five-act tragicomedy in the new Fletcherian mode — suffering, apparent death, and restoration — with the page's disguise and the citizens' rising as its hinges.
principal_characters: Philaster; Arethusa; Bellario (Euphrasia); the King of Sicily; Pharamond; Megra; Dion; Cleremont; Thrasiline; the citizens
meter_and_prosody: The supple Beaumont–Fletcher blank verse — run-on, conversational, and swift — that set the style of the Caroline stage.
historical_context: Performed by the King's Men about 1609–10 and printed in 1620; its popularity (it was the company's signature new play) made the partnership's name and the tragicomic genre's fortune.
literary_significance: The play that founded the Beaumont–Fletcher tragicomedy — the mode that would rule the English stage for the next fifty years.
attribution_notes: Jointly by Beaumont and Fletcher; the division of scenes is broadly agreed though not certain.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1620. Standard edition: Philaster, ed. Andrew Gurr (Revels, 1969).

title: The Maid's Tragedy
description: Beaumont and Fletcher's tragedy of honour: Amintor, commanded by the king, breaks his vow to Aspatia and marries Evadne — who is the king's secret mistress; Evadne's repentance, her murder of the king in the bedchamber, and Amintor's and Aspatia's deaths follow, in the play's double catastrophe of the marriage bed and the wedding night turned funeral.
plot_or_argument: The wedding night reveals Evadne's secret; Amintor's honour forbids revenge on the king; Aspatia, disguised as her own brother, takes the duel's death-blow from Amintor; Evadne, converted by her brother Melantius, kills the king; and the last act's cascade — Evadne's rejection, Aspatia's death, Amintor's suicide — empties the court of its lovers.
narrative_structure: A five-act tragedy of honour in the Senecan manner, with the bedchamber murder and the double suicide as its symmetrical climaxes.
principal_characters: Amintor; Evadne; Aspatia; Melantius; the King; Calianax; Lysippus; Diphilus; the Ladies; the masquers
meter_and_prosody: The fluent tragic verse of the partnership, with Evadne's and Aspatia's great speeches as its heights.
historical_context: Performed by the King's Men about 1610–11 and printed in 1619; its king-killing and bedchamber horrors made it the most talked-of tragedy of its decade.
literary_significance: The strongest of the Beaumont–Fletcher tragedies — the play in which the partnership's courtly polish met the Jacobean taste for blood.
attribution_notes: Jointly by Beaumont and Fletcher; the division of scenes is debated.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1619. Standard edition: The Maid's Tragedy, ed. T. W. Craik (Revels, 1988).

title: The Knight of the Burning Pestle
description: Beaumont's mock-romance of the citizen audience: a grocer and his wife, watching the play 'The London Merchant', demand that their apprentice Rafe act the part of a knight errant; the 'Knight of the Burning Pestle' then rides his adventures through Waltham Forest and the giant Barbaroso's barber shop, while the merchant play and the citizens' interruptions double and parody each other to the final, multiple endings.
plot_or_argument: The Citizen and his Wife interrupt the Prologue and hijack the play; Rafe's quests — the dainty damsel, the giants, the adventure of the barber — alternate with the merchant comedy of Venturewell, Jasper, and Luce; the plots collide at the mock-death of Rafe ('for the honor of Knights') and the play ends with the citizens' epilogue and the players' revenge on their audience.
narrative_structure: A play-within-a-play satire in which the audience is on stage from the start — the first burlesque of the English theatre's own conventions, including the romance, the city comedy, and the 'lamentable' death scene.
principal_characters: the Citizen; his Wife; Rafe (the Knight of the Burning Pestle); George (the apprentice); Venturewell; Jasper; Luce; Humphrey; Merrythought; Mistress Merrythought; Barbaroso the barber; the players
meter_and_prosody: Mixed verse and prose, with the ballad metres of Rafe's adventures and the songs of old Merrythought ('Nose, nose, jolly red nose') as its parodic instruments.
historical_context: First performed by the Children of the Revels at Blackfriars about 1607, where it failed; revived by the Queen's Revels boys and printed in 1613; it mocks the citizen taste that The Shoemaker's Holiday had flattered.
literary_significance: The first great English theatrical burlesque — the ancestor of Sheridan's Critic and of every later play about the audience's power over the stage.
attribution_notes: Generally assigned to Beaumont alone (perhaps with Fletcher's help); the 1613 title page names only Beaumont.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1613. Standard edition: The Knight of the Burning Pestle, ed. Sheldon P. Zitner (Revels, 1984).

title: A New Way to Pay Old Debts
description: Massinger's comedy of the extortioner's fall: Sir Giles Overreach, who has swallowed the estates of his neighbours through mortgage and fraud, plots the marriage of his daughter Margaret to the young Lord Lovell; the conspiracy of the just — Welborne's recovery of his lands, Lady Allworth's pretended favour, and the servants' evidence — brings Overreach to the mad scene in which he is dragged off 'in a frenzy', his schemes destroyed and his daughter married to the man she loves.
plot_or_argument: Welborne, ruined by Overreach, is raised by Lady Allworth's courtesy and wins his lands back through Overreach's own greed; Overreach forces Margaret toward Lovell, who instead promotes her marriage to Allworth; the double exposure — the deeds and the daughter's defiance — breaks the extortioner; and the final scene's madness ('The devil has left his shape') closes the comedy on the ruin of the usurer.
narrative_structure: A five-act city comedy of the Jonsonian school, built on the double plot of Welborne's restoration and Margaret's marriage, with Overreach's fall as its moral engine.
principal_characters: Sir Giles Overreach; Frank Welborne; Margaret Overreach; Tom Allworth; Lady Allworth; Lord Lovell; Justice Greedy; Marrall; Will-do; the parson; the servants
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse and prose in Massinger's careful, moral style, with Overreach's mad scene as the great actor's moment it became.
historical_context: Written about 1625 and printed in 1633; Overreach was modelled on the notorious extortioner Sir Giles Mompesson; the role became the property of the great actors from the Restoration to the twentieth century.
literary_significance: The last great comedy of the pre-Civil War stage — and the vehicle of one of the English theatre's most durable villains.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1633. Standard edition: A New Way to Pay Old Debts, ed. T. W. Craik (New Mermaids, 1964).

title: A Woman Killed with Kindness
description: Heywood's domestic tragedy: the Yorkshire gentleman Frankford discovers his wife Anne's adultery with his guest Wendoll; instead of blood, he punishes her by banishment to a distant manor — kindness as execution — where she starves herself to death and dies on the marriage bed in the play's final scene, while the sub-plot of Sir Charles Mountford's imprisonment and Susan's sacrifice runs its parallel course.
plot_or_argument: Frankford's friendship with Wendoll becomes the adulterer's entry; the discovery through the cards, the quiet banishment, and Anne's self-starvation follow; the sub-plot of Sir Charles's debt, his sister's sacrifice to Sir Francis Acton, and the reversal of fortune ends in the double marriage of the close, with Anne's deathbed forgiveness as the tragedy's summit.
narrative_structure: A two-plot domestic tragedy — the Frankford household and the Mountfords — in Heywood's plain middle style, the first English tragedy of the ordinary marriage.
principal_characters: Frankford; Anne Frankford; Wendoll; Sir Charles Mountford; Susan Mountford; Sir Francis Acton; Shafton; Nicholas; the servants
meter_and_prosody: Plain, unadorned blank verse and prose — deliberately domestic, without the Senecan heights of the revenge school.
historical_context: Performed by Worcester's Men in 1603 and printed in 1607; it founded the genre of domestic tragedy that runs through Arden of Faversham's earlier example to Lillo, Ibsen, and the modern theatre.
literary_significance: The masterpiece of English domestic tragedy — the play that brought the marriage bed, not the court, to the centre of the tragic stage.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1607. Standard edition: A Woman Killed with Kindness, ed. Brian Scobie (New Mermaids, 1985).

title: Arden of Faversham
alternative_titles: The Lamentable and True Tragedy of Master Arden of Faversham
description: The anonymous domestic tragedy of the real murder of Thomas Arden of Faversham in 1551: his wife Alice and her lover Mosby hire a succession of bungling assassins — Black Will and Shakebag among them — whose attempts fail comically until the murder is done in Arden's own house; the killers are caught, and the play ends with the executions and Alice's burning, 'the sin of murder' its homiletic close.
plot_or_argument: Alice's adultery and Arden's blindness to it set the plot; the hired murders fail through fog, chance, and cowardice; the final ambush in the parlour succeeds; the discovery of the body, the flight of the murderers, and the punishment of all — including Alice, who dies 'bewailed' only by her guilt — complete the tragedy's documentary arc.
narrative_structure: A five-act tragedy built directly on Holinshed's account of the real 1551 murder, with the comic failures of the assassins as its counterpoint to the horror.
principal_characters: Thomas Arden; Alice Arden; Mosby; Black Will; Shakebag; Greene; Michael; Franklin; the Mayor of Faversham; Susan; Clarke the painter
meter_and_prosody: A plain, powerful verse (and prose) of the provincial scene — the play's very anonymity has invited attribution to Shakespeare, Kyd, and others.
historical_context: Printed in 1592 and performed by the Admiral's Men; based on the notorious Faversham murder of 1551 as told in Holinshed; it is the first English play of a real, recent, and domestic crime.
literary_significance: The founding text of English domestic tragedy — the first play to make an English household and an English murder the matter of tragedy.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; attributions to Kyd, Shakespeare, and others have been proposed but none is proven.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1592. Standard edition: Arden of Faversham, ed. M. L. Wine (Revels, 1973).

title: A Yorkshire Tragedy
description: The short anonymous (or Shakespeare-attributed) domestic tragedy of the real Walter Calverley murders of 1605: the gambling squire, his estate devoured by dice, stabs his wife and murders two of his children in their beds — the third wounded — and, taken by his servants, goes to his execution repentant, the play compressing the whole crime into its ten scenes.
plot_or_argument: The Husband's ruin at dice and the Wife's pleas frame the catastrophe; the murders of the children and the wounding of the wife are staged with brutal directness; the servants' arrest and the Husband's repentance before the officers close the play, with the real crime's ballads and pamphlets as its documentary frame.
narrative_structure: A one-act domestic tragedy in ten scenes, built on the pamphlet accounts of the Calverley murders of 1605.
principal_characters: the Husband (Walter Calverley); the Wife; the Master of the College (the Husband's brother); the Knight; the servants; the officers
meter_and_prosody: Verse and prose of violent economy — the play's brevity is its instrument of shock.
historical_context: Performed by the King's Men about 1608 and printed the same year as 'written by W. Shakespeare' — an attribution now generally rejected, though the question remains open; it was one of four plays in the 1608 quarto whose title page claimed Shakespeare's name.
literary_significance: The most compressed of the domestic tragedies — ten scenes of crime and repentance that test the limits of the genre's documentary power.
attribution_notes: The 1608 title page names Shakespeare, an attribution now generally rejected by scholarship; the author is unknown.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1608. Standard edition: A Yorkshire Tragedy, ed. Keith Sturgess (in Three Elizabethan Domestic Tragedies, Penguin, 1969).

title: Mucedorus
alternative_titles: A Most Pleasant Comedy of Mucedorus, the King's Son of Valentia
description: The anonymous romance-comedy that became the best-selling play of the age: Mucedorus, prince of Valentia, disguises himself as a shepherd to woo the princess Amadine of Aragon; the wild man Bremo, the bear, and the clown Mouse fill the forest adventures; and the play ends with the lovers' marriage, Bremo's defeat, and — in the 1610 revision — the added scenes of the bear's death and the king's feast.
plot_or_argument: Mucedorus leaves court in disguise; Amadine, fleeing the wild man Bremo, meets the shepherd; the courtship, the clown Mouse's cowardice, and the fight with Bremo follow; the play moves to the recognition and the wedding, with the 1610 additions (attributed to Shakespeare in the printed text) supplying the bear scene and the final entertainment.
narrative_structure: A five-act romance-comedy in the old-fashioned mode — disguised prince, wild man, clown — that its very simplicity made immortal in the provinces.
principal_characters: Mucedorus; Amadine; Bremo the wild man; Mouse the clown; the King of Aragon; Segasto; Envy, Comedy (the Induction); the bear; the King of Valentia
meter_and_prosody: Loose blank verse and prose, with the clown's jests and the Induction's debate of Envy and Comedy.
historical_context: Probably written about 1590, printed in 1598, and revised in 1610 with additions 'newly set forth'; it went through more editions before 1642 than any other play, its Shakespearian ascription a bookseller's later device.
literary_significance: The most popular play of the early Stuart stage — the romance-comedy that travelled England with the strolling players.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; the 1610 additions were claimed for Shakespeare by the publisher, an ascription now generally rejected.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1598 (revised 1610). Standard edition: Mucedorus, ed. Arvin H. Jupin (in A Critical Old-Spelling Edition, 1987).

title: The Witch of Edmonton
description: Dekker, Ford, and Rowley's tragicomedy of the real Elizabeth Sawyer, hanged as a witch at Edmonton in 1621: the old woman, cursed and beaten by her neighbours, sells herself to the devil in the shape of the black dog Tom; the parallel plot of the bigamist Frank Thorney and his murders runs alongside; and the play ends with Sawyer's execution and Thorney's confession, the village's two sins joined in one scaffold.
plot_or_argument: Old Banks's curses and the villagers' cruelty drive Sawyer to the dog Tom; her witchcraft plagues the village while Frank Thorney, secretly married, stabs his second wife Susan and is pursued by the law; the two plots converge in the final acts, where Sawyer's repentance and execution and Thorney's scaffold confession close the play on the wages of desperation and greed.
narrative_structure: A two-plot tragicomedy — the witch and the bigamist — built on the documentary record of the 1621 trial and the pamphlet of Henry Goodcole.
principal_characters: Elizabeth Sawyer; the Dog (Tom); Frank Thorney; Susan Carter; Winnifred; Old Thorney; Sir Arthur Clarington; Cuddy Banks; Old Carter; Katherine Carter; the Justice
meter_and_prosody: The three authors' mixed verse and prose, with Sawyer's curses and the dog's speeches as the play's remembered scenes.
historical_context: Performed at court in December 1621, within months of the real Sawyer's execution in April of that year; printed in 1658; its sympathetic witch answered the decade's pamphlet wars over witchcraft.
literary_significance: The most humane of the English witch plays — the first to make the witch's persecution, not her malice, the tragedy.
attribution_notes: By Dekker, Ford, and Rowley, as stated on the title page; the division of scenes is partly conjectural.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1658. Standard edition: The Witch of Edmonton, ed. Peter Corbin and Douglas Sedge (Revels, 1986).
